question: Astronomer Tycho Brahe lost the tip of his nose in a sword duel with a cousin over a math argument. For the rest of his life, what did he wear to cover it?
answer: A fake metal nose-tip
choices: A fake metal nose-tip
A black silk eye-patch
A bright red wig-cap
A carved wood mask
context: The 1566 duel with Manderup Parsberg (over who was the better mathematician) cost Tycho his nose-tip. He wore a prosthetic of brass, and possibly silver and gold for special occasions, glued on with paste, for the rest of his life.

question: For 2,000 years people were sure the planets moved in perfect circles. Studying Mars for years, Johannes Kepler found their true path is a slightly squashed circle. What is that oval shape called?
answer: An ellipse
choices: An ellipse
A triangle
A spiral
A square
context: Kepler announced his first law in 1609: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, not circles, with the Sun off to one side at a focus. He cracked it using Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars, the hardest planet to fit to a circle.

question: Isaac Newton said that watching one ordinary thing fall in his mother's garden set him thinking about why the Moon stays in the sky. What fell?
answer: An apple from a tree
choices: An apple from a tree
A bucket down a well
A bird from its nest
A leaf off a vine
context: Newton told the apple story late in life to several people, including his biographer William Stukeley. The tree at Woolsthorpe Manor still stands. The same force that pulls an apple down, he reasoned, reaches all the way to the Moon.

question: The story goes that Archimedes solved a king's puzzle while climbing into a bath and was so excited he ran outside without his clothes. What did he shout?
answer: Eureka — I've found it
choices: Eureka — I've found it
Stop that royal thief
Bring me the crown!
The bath is too cold
context: The tale, told by the Roman writer Vitruvius, has Archimedes realizing that his body pushed water out of the tub equal to its own volume, giving him a way to test if a crown was pure gold. 'Eureka' is Greek for 'I have found it.'

question: Thomas Edison tested thousands of materials looking for a light-bulb filament that would glow without burning up fast. About how many tries did he say it took?
answer: Thousands of failed tries
choices: Thousands of failed tries
Just three quick tries
Exactly one lucky try
No tries — he bought it
context: Edison's Menlo Park team tested thousands of filament materials before settling on carbonized bamboo for a long-lasting bulb in 1880. He is often quoted as saying he had not failed, but found many ways that would not work.

question: The famous story says young Galileo climbed a leaning tower in Pisa and dropped two balls of different weights to settle an argument. What did watchers see?
answer: Both balls landed together
choices: Both balls landed together
The heavy ball won easily
The light ball won easily
Both balls floated down
context: The tower tale comes from Galileo's student Vincenzo Viviani and may be embellished. But the physics is real: ignoring air, all objects fall at the same rate. Galileo argued this against Aristotle, who had taught heavier things fall faster.

question: Marie Curie kept tubes of her newly found element radium by her bed, and loved that they gave off a faint light in the dark. What did that eerie glow turn out to be a sign of?
answer: Dangerous radiation
choices: Dangerous radiation
Harmless candlelight
Trapped fireflies
Reflected moonlight
context: Curie called the glow beautiful and kept samples in her desk drawer. The radiation that caused it also made her ill; her notebooks are still so radioactive they are stored in lead-lined boxes and handlers sign a waiver to open them.

question: Benjamin Franklin wanted to prove that lightning was the same thing as the electric sparks in his lab. According to his account, what did he fly in a storm to test it?
answer: A kite with a metal key
choices: A kite with a metal key
A copper boat on a lake
A glass jar on a pole
A silver coin on a wire
context: Franklin described the 1752 experiment in a letter; he kept the kite under a shelter so he stayed dry and warned it was dangerous. A wet string can conduct charge, and others who copied it carelessly were killed. He invented the lightning rod from this work.

question: Visiting the sick Indian genius Srinivasa Ramanujan, mathematician G. H. Hardy mentioned he had ridden in a dull taxi numbered 1729. Ramanujan instantly disagreed it was dull. Why did he find 1729 special?
answer: It is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways
choices: It is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways
It was the exact year he had first arrived in the city of London
It was the room number of the hospital ward he was staying in
It was the page where his favorite math proof happened to appear
context: 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3. Hardy recalled the exchange as showing how every number seemed to be a personal friend of Ramanujan's. Such numbers are now called 'taxicab numbers' after this story.

question: The night before a pistol duel he expected to lose, 20-year-old French mathematician Evariste Galois stayed up writing furiously. What was he racing to get onto paper?
answer: His new mathematical ideas, before he could be killed
choices: His new mathematical ideas, before he could be killed
A long apology letter to the man he was about to fight
His last will leaving money to the French army
A map showing where he had buried a box of gold
context: Galois died from the duel wound on May 31, 1832. His scribbled pages, with notes like 'I have no time' in the margins, founded what we now call group theory — a whole branch of mathematics — years ahead of everyone else.

question: Physicist Wolfgang Pauli was so notorious for equipment mysteriously breaking the moment he walked into a lab that colleagues gave the joke a name. What did they call it?
answer: The Pauli Effect
choices: The Pauli Effect
The Pauli Theorem
The Pauli Constant
The Pauli Reaction
context: It was a running joke among physicists, not real science. One famous tale: a costly apparatus failed in Gottingen for no reason, and the experimenter later joked he was safe because Pauli was only passing through on a train. Pauli himself enjoyed the legend.

question: Henry Cavendish was so painfully shy he communicated with his servants by notes and added a back staircase to avoid people. Yet in 1798 he carefully measured one giant thing in his home lab. What did he basically 'weigh'?
answer: The whole planet Earth
choices: The whole planet Earth
The light from the Sun
The air in a sealed room
The heat of a candle
context: Using lead balls on a delicate twisting rod, Cavendish measured the tiny gravitational pull between masses. From that he calculated Earth's density, and so its mass. He was a recluse, but one of the most precise experimenters who ever lived.

question: Benjamin Banneker, a free Black American and self-taught mathematician, borrowed a pocket watch, took it apart, and studied the gears. What did he then carve entirely by hand?
answer: A working wooden clock
choices: A working wooden clock
A brass telescope lens
A small printing press
A ship's brass compass
context: Around 1753 Banneker built a striking clock almost entirely from hand-carved wood; it kept time for decades. Largely self-taught in astronomy, he later published almanacs and exchanged a famous letter on equality with Thomas Jefferson.

question: Michael Faraday left school at 13 and worked binding books. He educated himself by reading the very books he was binding. What humble job let this future great scientist into the famous Royal Institution?
answer: Lab assistant, washing bottles and taking notes
choices: Lab assistant, washing bottles and taking notes
Head professor of chemistry on his first day
Owner who bought the whole building outright
A wealthy donor who never did any work
context: Faraday sent bound notes from lectures to chemist Humphry Davy, who hired him as a bottle-washing assistant in 1813. With almost no formal math, Faraday went on to discover electromagnetic induction — the principle behind every electric generator.

question: To help his tax-collector father with endless sums, a teenage Blaise Pascal spent years building one of the first machines of its kind. What did the 'Pascaline' do?
answer: Add and subtract using turning gears
choices: Add and subtract using turning gears
Print whole books one page at a time
Tell the time by the position of the Sun
Send messages by flashing mirrors
context: Pascal began the device around 1642 at age 19. Dialed wheels carried the tens automatically, like a car odometer. He built about 50 of them. A unit of pressure is now named the pascal in his honor.

question: A quiet Austrian monk named Gregor Mendel spent eight years breeding and counting around 28,000 pea plants in his monastery garden. What was he carefully tracking from parent to offspring?
answer: How traits like tall or short are passed down
choices: How traits like tall or short are passed down
How fast the garden weeds could spread
How much honey his beehives produced
How the weather changed the soil color
context: Mendel's pea counts (1856-1863) revealed dominant and recessive traits — the foundation of genetics. The scientific world ignored his paper for about 34 years; it was rediscovered around 1900, long after he had died as an abbot.

question: Evariste Galois failed his college entrance exam twice, was thrown in prison for his politics, and at 20 was shot in a duel. The night before, he scrawled his discoveries in a letter, begging a friend to get them published. What did those frantic pages eventually give the world?
answer: Group theory, a major new branch of mathematics
choices: Group theory, a major new branch of mathematics
The first accurate map of the planet Mars
A cure for the disease that killed his father
The design for the first steam locomotive
context: Galois died May 31, 1832. His ideas about the symmetry of equations explained why no formula can solve all 5th-degree equations, and seeded group theory, now used in physics, chemistry, and cryptography. Mathematicians took years to even understand his notes.

question: In 1847 Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis noticed mothers died far more often in the ward run by doctors than the one run by midwives. He realized the doctors came straight from dissecting corpses, and ordered them to wash hands in chlorine water. Deaths plunged. How did fellow doctors react?
answer: They mocked and rejected him, and he died ignored in an asylum
choices: They mocked and rejected him, and he died ignored in an asylum
They cheered and made him head of every hospital in Europe
They gave him the first-ever medical Nobel Prize that year
They quietly copied him and gave him no credit but stayed friends
context: Semmelweis could not explain WHY it worked — germ theory came later from Pasteur and Koch — so colleagues dismissed his statistics. Insulted and broken, he was committed to an asylum and died there in 1865, possibly beaten by guards. He was vindicated only after his death.

question: Edmond Halley, the comet astronomer, visited Isaac Newton and asked a question about planetary orbits. Newton's stunning answer was hidden in unpublished work. What did Halley then do to make sure the world saw it?
answer: He paid out of his own pocket to publish Newton's masterwork
choices: He paid out of his own pocket to publish Newton's masterwork
He stole the papers and published them under his own name
He locked the papers away so no rival could ever read them
He challenged Newton to a duel over who deserved the credit
context: In 1684 Halley prompted Newton to write up his theory of gravity. The Royal Society had no money (it had overspent on a book about fish), so Halley personally funded the printing of the Principia (1687) — one of the most important books in the history of science.

question: Looking at a world map, Alfred Wegener saw that South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces, with matching fossils on both sides. In 1912 he proposed the continents had once been joined and drifted apart. How did geologists treat the idea for the next 50 years?
answer: They dismissed it as nonsense until seafloor evidence proved him right
choices: They dismissed it as nonsense until seafloor evidence proved him right
They accepted it at once and renamed the continents after him
They proved it false, and science still rejects drifting continents
They classified it as a military secret for several decades
context: Wegener could not explain HOW continents move, so the idea was scorned. In the 1960s, seafloor spreading and matching magnetic stripes on the ocean floor confirmed plate tectonics. Wegener had died on a Greenland expedition in 1930, 30 years before being vindicated.

question: Mathematician Georg Cantor proved something so strange that famous colleagues called it a 'disease' and blocked his career: there are different SIZES of infinity, and some infinities are bigger than others. Which set did he prove is the LARGER infinity?
answer: All the decimal numbers between 0 and 1
choices: All the decimal numbers between 0 and 1
All the whole counting numbers 1, 2, 3...
All the even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8...
All the days in one hundred years
context: Cantor showed the counting numbers can't be matched one-to-one with the decimals — the decimals are a strictly bigger infinity. Leopold Kronecker attacked him brutally. Cantor suffered depression and died in a sanatorium in 1918; today his set theory underpins all of mathematics.

question: Nikola Tesla's alternating current (AC) could send power over long distances, threatening Thomas Edison's direct current (DC) business. In the 'War of the Currents,' how did the Edison side try to scare the public away from AC?
answer: By publicly electrocuting animals to call AC deadly
choices: By publicly electrocuting animals to call AC deadly
By proving in court that AC could not light a bulb
By buying every AC generator and destroying them
By showing AC made people's hair fall out over time
context: In the 1880s-90s Edison's camp staged demonstrations electrocuting animals to brand AC as dangerous, and AC was even used to design the first electric chair. AC won anyway because it transmits efficiently; Tesla and George Westinghouse lit the 1893 World's Fair and Niagara Falls.

question: Many scientists believed rotting meat could spontaneously create maggots and microbes from nothing. Louis Pasteur designed a clever curved 'swan-neck' flask to settle it. What did his broth show?
answer: It stayed clear until outside germs were let in
choices: It stayed clear until outside germs were let in
It grew new life even with all air blocked out
It turned to solid gold after several months
It boiled by itself whenever the Sun rose
context: The curved neck let air in but trapped dust and microbes in the bend. The sterilized broth stayed clear for months; tip it to wet the neck, and it spoiled. Pasteur's 1859 experiment helped kill the idea of spontaneous generation and supported germ theory.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev was arranging the known chemical elements by their properties. He claimed the full pattern came to him in a dream. Boldly, he left GAPS in his 1869 table. What were those empty spaces for?
answer: Undiscovered elements, whose traits he predicted
choices: Undiscovered elements, whose traits he predicted
Pure decoration to keep the chart looking neat
Elements he thought were too dangerous to name
Old mistakes he never got around to erasing
context: Mendeleev predicted the properties of missing elements like gallium and germanium with startling accuracy; when they were found, his periodic table was vindicated. He reportedly saw the arrangement in a dream after days of work shuffling element cards.

question: Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz both claimed to have invented calculus first, sparking a bitter feud across Europe. The Royal Society set up a 'neutral' committee to judge who deserved credit, and its report sided with Newton. Decades later, historians found a secret. What had Newton, as president of the Society, actually done?
answer: He secretly wrote the supposedly impartial report himself
choices: He secretly wrote the supposedly impartial report himself
He bribed Leibniz to drop the claim and stay silent
He destroyed all of Leibniz's letters and notebooks
He stole the idea from a student and blamed Leibniz
context: Newton was president of the Royal Society when it formed the 1712 committee. He drafted its findings, the Commercium Epistolicum, anonymously, and even wrote an unsigned review praising it. Historians now agree both men developed calculus independently; Leibniz's notation is the one we still use.

question: Ludwig Boltzmann argued that heat and disorder come from the motion of countless tiny atoms — but many leading scientists of his day didn't even believe atoms were real, and attacked him for years. Despairing, he took his own life in 1906. What did admirers later carve on his gravestone to honor his great idea?
answer: His equation linking disorder to atoms: S = k log W
choices: His equation linking disorder to atoms: S = k log W
A carving of the leaning tower he loved to visit
The full list of every award he had ever won
A poem he had written about the stars as a boy
context: Boltzmann's formula connects entropy (S, a measure of disorder) to the number of microscopic arrangements (W) of atoms. Critics like Ernst Mach doubted atoms existed. Within a few years of his death, Einstein's and Perrin's work on Brownian motion proved atoms real, vindicating him.

question: Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to capture 'Photo 51,' a stunning image hinting at DNA's shape. Without her knowledge, a colleague showed the photo to James Watson, who later said it was a key clue. When Watson, Crick, and Wilkins won the 1962 Nobel Prize for DNA's structure, why was Franklin not included?
answer: She had died in 1958, and Nobels are not awarded after death
choices: She had died in 1958, and Nobels are not awarded after death
She had publicly refused to accept any scientific prize
She had moved on and quit doing science altogether
She had been proven to fake the famous photograph
context: Maurice Wilkins showed Franklin's Photo 51 to Watson without her permission in 1953. Franklin died of ovarian cancer at 37, likely linked to her X-ray work. Nobel rules bar posthumous awards, so the 1962 prize went to the three living men; her crucial role is now widely recognized.

question: After the space shuttle Challenger exploded in 1986, physicist Richard Feynman joined the investigation. During a televised hearing, he did one simple thing with a clamp, a piece of rubber, and a glass of ice water that revealed the disaster's cause. What did his demonstration show?
answer: That cold made the rubber O-ring seals lose their springiness
choices: That cold made the rubber O-ring seals lose their springiness
That the fuel froze solid and could no longer burn
That the astronauts' radios stopped working in the cold
That ice on the wings made the shuttle too heavy
context: Feynman dunked a sample of the booster's rubber O-ring in ice water and showed it stayed squashed instead of springing back. Launch-day temperatures were near freezing; the stiff seals let hot gas escape. His simple demo cut through pages of bureaucratic explanation.

question: Antoine Lavoisier, often called the father of modern chemistry, named oxygen and showed that mass is conserved in chemical reactions. But he also worked as a tax collector for the French monarchy. During the French Revolution's Reign of Terror, what happened to him?
answer: He was beheaded by guillotine in 1794
choices: He was beheaded by guillotine in 1794
He fled to America and lived to old age
He was crowned head of a new science academy
He was exiled but kept all his laboratories
context: Lavoisier was executed on May 8, 1794, for his role in the tax-collecting Ferme generale. The judge reportedly said the Republic had no need of scientists. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange lamented that it took only a moment to cut off that head, and a hundred years might not produce another like it.

question: Nikola Tesla once worked for Thomas Edison, who allegedly promised him a huge bonus to improve his machines. When Tesla delivered and asked for the money, Edison reportedly laughed it off as an American joke. What did Tesla do next, and what system did he champion against Edison?
answer: He quit, and promoted alternating current (AC) power
choices: He quit, and promoted alternating current (AC) power
He stayed for years and copied Edison's direct current
He sued Edison and won ownership of the light bulb
He gave up engineering to become a stage magician
context: Tesla left Edison around 1885. His alternating-current system, backed by industrialist George Westinghouse, could transmit power efficiently over long distances and beat Edison's direct current in the 'War of the Currents.' Tesla held some 300 patents but died nearly broke in a New York hotel in 1943.

question: Young physicist Werner Heisenberg developed a startling idea about the tiny world of atoms: you cannot know both exactly where a particle is AND exactly how fast it is moving — the more you pin down one, the blurrier the other gets. Late-night arguments with his mentor Niels Bohr over this got so intense Heisenberg was reduced to tears. What is this principle now called?
answer: The uncertainty principle
choices: The uncertainty principle
The perfect-knowledge law
The total-certainty rule
The fixed-position rule
context: Heisenberg's 1927 uncertainty principle is a deep feature of quantum physics, not just a limit of our tools. He and Bohr clashed bitterly over how to interpret it while developing the 'Copenhagen interpretation.' Heisenberg won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics.

question: Charles Darwin worked out his theory of evolution by natural selection but sat on it for about 20 years, afraid of the uproar it would cause. Then a letter arrived from naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the islands of Southeast Asia. Why did the letter alarm Darwin?
answer: Wallace had independently reached the same theory
choices: Wallace had independently reached the same theory
Wallace threatened to expose Darwin as a fraud
Wallace claimed evolution had been disproven
Wallace demanded Darwin pay him for his notes
context: Wallace's 1858 letter outlined natural selection almost exactly as Darwin had. Friends arranged a joint presentation so both got credit, and Darwin rushed 'On the Origin of Species' into print in 1859. The two men remained on respectful terms despite the close call.

question: Hypatia of Alexandria was one of the ancient world's greatest mathematicians and astronomers, teaching geometry and the motions of the heavens to students who came from far away. She lectured publicly and advised city leaders at a time when very few women held such standing. Around the year 415, caught up in the violent political and religious strife tearing her city apart, what happened to her?
answer: A mob seized and murdered her in the street
choices: A mob seized and murdered her in the street
She retired quietly and lived to a great old age
She was crowned ruler of the whole city of Alexandria
She sailed to Rome and opened a famous new school
context: Hypatia edited mathematical works and built astronomical instruments. She was killed by a mob during a power struggle involving the Roman prefect Orestes and Bishop Cyril. Her death is often marked as a symbolic blow to the scholarly world of late-antique Alexandria; she became a lasting emblem of learning destroyed by mob violence.

question: Emmy Noether proved a theorem so important that it became a cornerstone of modern physics, linking nature's symmetries to its conservation laws — for example, why energy is conserved. Yet the University of Gottingen refused to let a woman become a paid lecturer. How did the great mathematician David Hilbert get around the ban so she could teach?
answer: He announced her lectures under his own name
choices: He announced her lectures under his own name
He paid her salary secretly from his own pocket
He disguised her as a male professor in class
He moved the entire department to another country
context: Hilbert reportedly snapped at the faculty senate that this was a university, not a bathhouse, when they objected to a woman teaching. Noether's theorem (1918) is fundamental to physics. As a Jewish woman, she was forced out by the Nazis in 1933 and emigrated to the United States, where she died in 1935.

question: Alan Turing helped invent the idea of the modern computer and led the British team that cracked Nazi Germany's 'Enigma' code at Bletchley Park, work credited with shortening World War II and saving many lives. Yet a few years after the war, the British government did something to this national hero because he was gay. What did the state do to him?
answer: It prosecuted him and forced him to undergo chemical treatment
choices: It prosecuted him and forced him to undergo chemical treatment
It awarded him the country's highest honor in public
It made him head of the national computer program
It paid him a large pension and a country estate
context: Convicted of 'gross indecency' in 1952, Turing was given hormone injections as an alternative to prison and stripped of his security clearance. He died in 1954 from cyanide poisoning, widely ruled a suicide. The UK government formally apologized in 2009, and the Queen granted a posthumous pardon in 2013.

question: The brilliant observer Tycho Brahe spent decades recording the most precise measurements of the planets ever made — but he was a poor mathematician. His assistant, Johannes Kepler, was a gifted mathematician but had little data of his own. According to the famous account, how did Kepler finally gain full access to Tycho's priceless records?
answer: Tycho died suddenly and Kepler inherited the data
choices: Tycho died suddenly and Kepler inherited the data
Tycho freely handed everything over as a gift
Kepler bought the records from a wealthy king
Kepler copied them in secret over many years
context: Tycho guarded his data jealously and fed it to Kepler in pieces. He died in 1601, days after an illness that legend links to a strained bladder at a banquet where etiquette kept him from leaving the table; modern theories also suggest other causes. Using Tycho's Mars observations, Kepler discovered that planets move in ellipses, his famous three laws.

question: Linus Pauling was perhaps the greatest chemist of his age and one of only a handful of people to win two unshared Nobel Prizes. In the race to find the structure of DNA, he rushed out a bold proposed structure in early 1953 — which turned out to be embarrassingly wrong. What mistake did the master chemist make?
answer: He proposed a three-strand helix, turned inside-out
choices: He proposed a three-strand helix, turned inside-out
He claimed that DNA was a simple flat square sheet
He insisted that DNA was made entirely of pure sugar
He argued that DNA did not exist in living cells at all
context: Pauling's triple-helix model put the phosphate backbone in the center and wasn't even acid, a basic chemistry error. Watson and Crick, partly spurred by the fear that Pauling would beat them, found the correct double helix months later in 1953. Pauling won Chemistry (1954) and Peace (1962) Nobels.

question: Leonhard Euler was the most prolific mathematician in history, writing so much that printers struggled to keep up for decades after his death. Remarkably, he did some of his most productive work during the last 17 years of his life despite a severe disability. What had happened to him?
answer: He had gone almost totally blind
choices: He had gone almost totally blind
He had completely lost his hearing
He could no longer use either hand
He had lost the ability to speak
context: Euler lost sight in one eye early and became nearly blind by 1771, yet his output INCREASED — he did calculations in his head and dictated to scribes. He produced work in calculus, number theory, and physics; the constant e and much modern notation come from him. He worked until the day he died in 1783.

question: The mathematician Paul Erdos had no home, no job, and almost no possessions. He traveled the world with a suitcase, showing up at fellow mathematicians' doors to work on problems, famously announcing that 'my brain is open.' He published with so many partners that mathematicians now playfully measure something in his honor. What do they count?
answer: Their 'Erdos number' — how many co-author steps link them to him
choices: Their 'Erdos number' — how many co-author steps link them to him
Their 'Erdos miles' — how far they traveled to meet him
Their 'Erdos coins' — the cash prizes he handed out
Their 'Erdos hours' — how long they argued with him
context: Erdos co-authored about 1,500 papers with over 500 collaborators, more than almost anyone in history. A direct co-author has an Erdos number of 1, their co-authors 2, and so on. He lived out of a suitcase, gave away his money as problem prizes, and worked on mathematics up to 19 hours a day until his death in 1996.

question: For decades, doctors were certain that stomach ulcers came from stress and spicy food, and that no germ could survive the stomach's acid. Australian researcher Barry Marshall was convinced a bacterium was the real cause, but no one would take his evidence seriously. In 1984, frustrated, he did something drastic to himself to prove it. What did he do?
answer: He drank a flask of the live bacteria
choices: He drank a flask of the live bacteria
He swallowed a tiny camera on a wire
He starved himself for a full month
He injected himself with strong acid
context: Marshall drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori and developed gastritis within days, then cured himself with antibiotics. He and pathologist Robin Warren had identified the bacterium in 1982 to widespread disbelief. They won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Medicine, and ulcers are now routinely cured with antibiotics.
